extra.message: Hardcoded weak JWT signing secret — Attacker forges valid JWTs for any user (including admin), bypassing authentication entirely. [verified: config.py sets SECRET_KEY='random', a trivially guessable static HS256 key used by encode_auth_token/decode_auth_token in user_model.py; anyone knowing it can forge JWTs for any sub including admin.]

Hardcoded weak JWT signing secret ('random') — Attacker forges JWTs for any user (including admin), fully bypassing authentication/authorization to read/modify/delete any account or book. [verified: config.py hardcodes SECRET_KEY='random'; user_model.py signs (line ~39) and verifies (line ~48) JWTs with it, and token_validator trusts the decoded sub as identity, fully bypassing authn/authz.]

SQL injection in get_user via username path parameter — Full read (and potentially write via stacked/boolean logic) of the users table including plaintext passwords, emails, and admin flags; complete authentication bypass / data exfiltration. [verified: get_user interpolates the unauthenticated path-parameter username into an f-string SQL query executed via db.session.execute(text(...)) when vuln=1 (default); no parameterization or auth on GET /users/v1/{username}.]

Broken Object Level Authorization (IDOR) on book secrets — Any authenticated user reads any other user's private book secret_content by guessing/enumerating titles. [verified: get_by_title's vuln branch (Book.query.filter_by(book_title=...)) lacks any user scope; the validated token's sub is unused for authorization, allowing cross-user enumeration of book secret_content.]

Unauthenticated database reset endpoint — Anonymous attacker drops all tables, destroying all data (denial of service / integrity loss). [verified: GET/POST /createdb maps to populate_db which calls db.drop_all() then db.create_all() with no security requirement in openapi3.yml and no token_validator/auth check in the handler, so any anonymous client can wipe and reseed the DB.]

Unauthenticated database reset endpoint — Anyone can wipe and reseed the database, destroying all user/book data (integrity/availability loss). [verified: The /createdb path block in openapi3.yml defines only a GET with responses and no bearerAuth/security, and populate_db performs db.drop_all();db.create_all() unauthenticated, allowing anonymous data destruction.]

Unauthenticated debug endpoint leaks all credentials — Anonymous attacker dumps every user's plaintext password, email, and admin flag, leading to full account/admin compromise. [verified: Duplicate of idx 2/9: unauthenticated /users/v1/_debug returns every user's plaintext password, email, and admin flag.]

Mass assignment of admin flag at registration — Privilege escalation: an anonymous attacker self-registers as admin and gains admin-only capabilities such as deleting any user. [verified: register_user binds client-supplied 'admin' to User(admin=admin) when vuln=1 (default); register_user_schema lacks additionalProperties:false and doesn't forbid 'admin', so an anonymous registrant can self-assign admin.]

Broken authorization allows changing any user's password — Account takeover: an authenticated attacker resets the password of arbitrary accounts (including admin) and hijacks them. [verified: In vuln mode update_password selects User.query.filter_by(username=username) from the path param rather than resp['sub'], with only token validity checked—any authenticated user resets any account's password.]

IDOR: change any user's password via username path parameter — Any authenticated user resets any other account's password (including admin), enabling full account takeover. [verified: Duplicate of idx 1/8/17: IDOR in update_password selecting target by path username in vuln mode with no ownership check.]

Unauthorized password change of arbitrary user (IDOR) — Any authenticated user can overwrite the password of any other account (including admin) and take it over. [verified: Duplicate of idx 1: update_password uses path username instead of token sub in vuln mode with no ownership/role check, enabling arbitrary password change.]

Flask debug mode enabled in production — Stack trace/source disclosure and potential remote code execution via the Werkzeug interactive debugger console. [verified: app.py line 17 runs vuln_app.run(host='0.0.0.0', port=5000, debug=True), enabling the Werkzeug interactive debugger and verbose tracebacks on all network interfaces, enabling source disclosure and potential RCE.]

Flask debug mode enabled on network-exposed app — Verbose stack traces leak internals; the interactive debugger can allow remote code execution if the PIN is bypassed. [verified: Confirmed: vuln_app.run(host='0.0.0.0', port=5000, debug=True) binds to 0.0.0.0 with debug=True, exposing the interactive debugger and verbose stack traces to network clients.]

Plaintext password storage — Any DB read (via SQLi, debug endpoint, or DB access) immediately exposes usable credentials; no protection if database leaks. [verified: User.password is a plain String column set directly from request data and compared as `request_data.get('password') == user.password` in login_user; no hashing/salting anywhere, init_db_users seeds plaintext 'pass1'.]

Plaintext password storage — Any database/file disclosure (or the debug endpoint/SQLi) immediately reveals usable credentials; no defense against credential theft. [verified: Passwords stored as raw String and compared in plaintext in login_user; no hashing at rest, so any DB/debug disclosure yields usable credentials.]

Plaintext password storage — Any database read (via the SQLi above, the debug endpoint, file access, or backup leak) immediately discloses all user passwords with no cracking required. [verified: register_user sets user.password directly from request body and login compares cleartext; init_db_users seeds plaintext passwords — credentials stored in SQLite in cleartext.]

Passwords stored in plaintext at rest — Any DB read (via SQLi, debug endpoint, or file access) yields all users' cleartext passwords, enabling account takeover and credential reuse attacks. [verified: json_debug() returns the plaintext password field and is exposed via the debug endpoint regardless of vuln flag; passwords are stored unhashed.]

Plaintext password serialized in debug user JSON — Anyone (no auth) reading the debug output obtains every user's cleartext password and admin flag, enabling full account takeover including the admin account. [verified: json_debug() in user_model.py:64 serializes the plaintext 'password' and 'admin' fields, and is reached via get_all_users_debug() -> debug() at the unauthenticated /users/v1/_debug endpoint (no token_validator in view, no security in openapi3.yml), leaking all credentials including admin.]

Per-user book secret stored in plaintext — Database compromise (or the SQLi/debug paths) discloses all users' secret_content in cleartext. [verified: api_views/books.py:36 writes request_data.get('secret') into Book.secret_content, and models/books_model.py defines secret_content as a plain db.String(128) column with no encryption, so the asset is stored in cleartext at rest.]

Missing authentication on user lookup route — Unauthenticated users can enumerate accounts and reach the SQL injection sink. [verified: Duplicate of idx 13: get_by_username route has no bearerAuth in spec and no code token check, exposing user lookup and the SQLi entry point unauthenticated.]

Missing rate limiting / brute-force protection on auth endpoints — Attacker can brute-force credentials or password-reset/registration endpoints without restriction. [verified: Duplicate of idx 5/12: no rate limiting/lockout on auth endpoints; login compares plaintext passwords with no throttling.]

Username/password enumeration via distinct login errors — Attacker can enumerate valid usernames to focus credential-stuffing/brute-force. [verified: Duplicate of idx 3: distinct login error messages in vuln mode enable username enumeration.]

Regular-expression denial of service (ReDoS) in email validation — A single crafted email value can pin a CPU and stall/deny the service for other requests. [verified: Duplicate of idx 4/11: catastrophic-backtracking email regex over attacker-controlled request_data.get('email').]

Unescaped user input in hand-built JSON error responses — Attacker-controlled content can corrupt/forge the JSON response body and inject fields, potentially confusing clients. [verified: Duplicate of idx 6: error_message_helper builds JSON via unescaped string concatenation of user-influenced messages.]

Verbose error/exception object returned in token response — Leaks internal error/implementation details to clients and produces malformed auth flow that can aid an attacker. [verified: encode_auth_token catches all exceptions and returns the exception object, which login_user places into the JSON auth_token; however SECRET_KEY is static and jwt.encode rarely raises, limiting real disclosure to a malformed-flow/info-exposure nit.]
